card.title: Bacterial cell and T4 phage — Gram walls, growth curve, lytic cycle

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Two cells textbooks keep confusing: the bacterial cell — naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall, no nucleus — and the virus, which is not a cell at all: nucleic acid in a protein capsid, inert until it hijacks a host. Monera covers the first; the T4 bacteriophage's lytic cycle is the NEB model for the second.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: Growth: lag → log (N = N₀·2ⁿ) → stationary → death  ·  Gram +ve: thick peptidoglycan (+ mesosome) → purple  ·  Gram −ve: thin peptidoglycan + LPS outer membrane → pink  ·  Lytic cycle: Adsorption → Penetration → Biosynthesis → Assembly → Release

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: The Gram result is a property of the wall, not the species — a thick peptidoglycan layer retains crystal violet (Gram +ve), a thin layer under an LPS outer membrane washes out (Gram −ve). Endospores appear only when nutrients run out. A virus needs a living host cell with the right receptors, and cyanobacterial nitrogen fixation needs the anaerobic heterocyst.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Mycoplasma has no wall at all and is the smallest living cell; Archaebacteria (Halobacterium, Methanobacterium, Thermoplasma) live in extreme habitats; an endospore is a survival structure, NOT reproduction — the standard MCQ trap; a virus carries DNA or RNA, never both; cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) are photosynthetic prokaryotes, not true algae; the 'are viruses alive?' debate wants both sides — no metabolism of their own, yet they replicate and evolve.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Growth numerical (unit exercise): a broth starts with 100 cells and generation time is 30 min. After 3 h = 180 min → n = 180/30 = 6 generations → N = 100 × 2⁶ = 6,400 cells. Lytic sequence in words: T4 attaches by tail fibres → injects DNA through the wall → host machinery makes phage parts → parts assemble → lysozyme bursts the cell and ~100–200 phage escape.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: One description never fits all bacteria: Mycoplasma defeats the wall-based schemes, obligate anaerobes die in air, and 'prokaryote = simple' collapses in front of plasmids, mesosomes and signal systems. And because viruses sit outside every kingdom, the five-kingdom table cannot place them — they are classified by nucleic acid type and host instead.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive the growth law from binary fission: one cell → two after one generation → four after two → N = N₀·2ⁿ. To pull n back out of a count, invert it: n = log₂(N/N₀). Then derive the lytic cycle as one causal chain — without adsorption no entry, without the host's ribosomes no biosynthesis, and without assembly and release the phage never reaches the next cell.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Strings: shapes are C-B-S-S (cocci, bacilli, spirilla, spirochaetes); growth is L-L-S-D; lytic is A-P-B-A-R; genetic exchange is C-T-T (conjugation, transformation, transduction). Virus = V-O-I (Very small, Obligate, Infectious). Remember 'endo = survival, not reproduction', and read Gram −ve as 'thin wall + LPS = pink'.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: NEB-style (unit practice bank): draw and label a T4 bacteriophage; describe the lytic cycle in five steps; differentiate DNA and RNA viruses with an example each; explain why viruses are not living organisms; tabulate Gram +ve and Gram −ve walls; state the role of plasmids; explain how rDNA technology makes human insulin in E. coli (isolate → cut → ligate → transform → select → express → harvest).
